title: SAT
blurb: Grid headings and the scales you must use.

cards.definition: Assess clarity, intensity, and colour. Note bubbles or sediment if present.
Assess condition, intensity, and aroma characteristics. Identify faults before describing fruit.
Record sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol, body, flavour intensity, flavour characteristics, and finish.
State quality level and readiness for drinking / ageing potential.
Clear or hazy. Haze may be a fault or acceptable in an unfiltered wine.
Depth of colour on appearance: pale, medium, or deep.
Light, medium(−), medium, medium(+), or pronounced. Not the same scale as colour intensity.
How long flavour lasts after the wine is spat or swallowed: short, medium(−/+/none), or long.
Judged from balance, length, intensity, and complexity. Not personal liking.
Too young; can drink now but has potential for ageing; drink now, not suitable for ageing; or too old.
Choose one term from the row. Do not write a range.
If cork taint, oxidation, reduction, or volatile acidity dominate, name the fault and the wine is faulty.
Sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol, and body. These frame flavour and drive conclusions.

title: Vine and climate
blurb: Plant, heat, and the growing season.

cards.definition: The species used for almost all wine production.
A root-feeding insect that kills vinifera on its own roots. Control is grafting onto resistant rootstocks.
Usually a non-vinifera or hybrid root. Chosen for phylloxera resistance, soil, and vigour.
Leaves convert sunlight to sugar. Sugar ripens fruit and later ferments to alcohol.
The long-term temperature, rainfall, and sunlight pattern of a region. It decides which grapes can ripen.
Conditions in a given year. The main cause of vintage variation.
Growing-season mean about 16.5°C or below. Higher acidity, lighter body, if the fruit still ripens.
Growing-season mean about 16.5–18.5°C. Many classic European still-wine regions sit here.
Growing-season mean about 18.5–21°C. Riper fruit, higher alcohol, lower acidity, fuller body.
Gap between daytime and night-time temperature. Cool nights slow acid loss while days still ripen flavour.
Gap between the hottest and coldest months. Continental sites have a shorter, more intense growing season.
Can kill bursting buds and wipe the crop. Site, late pruning, and frost protection are the usual responses.
Needed for photosynthesis and growth. Too little stops ripening; too much dilutes fruit and raises disease pressure.
The permanent shape of the vine on a trellis or as a free-standing bush.
The annual cut that sets bud number and therefore this year's potential yield.
Arranging leaves and bunches for light, airflow, and even ripening, and to limit disease.
Crop size, usually tonnes/ha or hl/ha. High yield can dilute flavour; very low yield can delay ripening.
Applied water. Common in dry climates; restricted or banned in many European appellations.
Vertical shoot positioning: shoots trained upright into a thin curtain of leaves.
Untrained or minimally trained, no high trellis. Used in hot, dry, or windy sites and for old vines.
Removing some unripe bunches so remaining fruit can ripen more fully.
The last vineyard decision. It fixes sugar, acid, tannin ripeness, and flavour.
Certified limits on synthetic herbicides, insecticides, and fertilisers. It does not by itself define wine style.
Organic rules plus specified preparations and a farm as a closed system. Again, not a style guarantee.
Vines per hectare. Higher density often means more competition, lower yield per vine, and a need for more labour.
Crushing splits berries. Pressing separates juice or wine from skins and seeds.
Selected Saccharomyces inoculated for a reliable, complete ferment.
Yeast already on grapes or in the winery. Less control; can add complexity or risk a stuck ferment.
Typically cool (about 12–22°C) to retain fresh fruit aromas.
Typically warmer (about 20–32°C) to extract colour, tannin, and flavour from skins.
Lactic acid bacteria convert malic acid to lactic acid. Standard for most reds; optional for whites. Softens acidity and can add buttery notes if diacetyl is present.
Dead yeast cells. Ageing on lees can add body and flavour; bâtonnage (stirring) increases contact.
Allow slow oxygen ingress and can add flavour (vanilla, clove, toast). New oak has more flavour than old; small barrels more than large.
Inert, easy to temperature-control, no oak flavour. Used to preserve primary fruit.
Antioxidant and antimicrobial. Used from harvest through bottling to protect the wine.
Time on skins. For reds this extracts colour, tannin, and flavour; for rosé it is short; for most whites it is little or none.
Intact berries in a CO2-rich environment. Intracellular fermentation gives low tannin and distinct banana/kirsch fruit. Used especially in Beaujolais.
Direct press, short maceration, or (less often, and in some regions only) blending red and white. Saignée is bleeding juice from a red ferment.

title: Wine law
blurb: PDO, PGI, and what a label may claim.

cards.definition: Protected Designation of Origin. The stricter EU geographic category: smaller area, defined grapes and production.
Protected Geographical Indication. Broader area and more flexible grape and winemaking rules than PDO.
Geographic indication outside the EU PDO/PGI ladder. Often defines place more than recipe.
National names that sit inside PDO (France AOC/AOP, Italy DOCG/DOC, Spain DO/DOCa).
Common on New World labels. EU PDO wines often omit variety because the place implies it.
Legally defined ageing in some countries (e.g. Spain, Italy). Unregulated marketing language in others.
Adding sugar (or must concentrate) before or during ferment to raise potential alcohol. Allowed in cooler EU zones, restricted or banned in warmer ones.
Adding acid, usually tartaric. More often permitted in warm regions; rules are specific to the country.
Many PDOs cap hl/ha. Lower legal maxima are used as one quality control.
If a vintage is stated, a high percentage of the wine must come from that harvest (exact % is set by law).
Names such as Champagne or Port may only be used for wine from that place, in markets that enforce the protection.
A common mandatory allergen-style statement when SO2 is above the legal threshold.
